title: Italy GP 2026: Practice Sessions Analysis & Race Predictions
summary: George Russell stitched together a theoretical 1:22.092 across the three Monza practice sessions — almost three tenths clear of Lewis Hamilton in our aggregated order. Ferrari owned FP1, but Mercedes took over from FP2 onward, while Max Verstappen quietly posted the most complete lap of the weekend despite skipping FP1. Our exclusive aggregated-vs-actual data points to a Russell pole and a tight Ferrari–McLaren fight behind.

sections.heading: The Headline: Russell Takes Command at the Temple of Speed
sections.content:
George Russell arrives at qualifying for the Italian Grand Prix as the man to beat. Combining his best sectors from all three practice sessions, the Mercedes driver's theoretical lap stands at 1:22.092 — a full 0.286s clear of Lewis Hamilton and 0.337s ahead of team-mate Kimi Antonelli. He also set the fastest actual lap of the weekend, a 1:22.219 in FP3, and topped both FP2 and FP3 outright. On a circuit where gaps are traditionally compressed by long straights, a near-three-tenth margin in ultimate potential is a statement.

It did not start that way. Ferrari opened their home weekend with a 1-2 in FP1, Charles Leclerc's 1:23.008 leading Hamilton by 0.173s and sending the tifosi into Friday evening with real hope. But from FP2 onward the picture shifted: Russell's 1:22.559 put Mercedes on top, and his FP3 run lowered the benchmark again. Leclerc's best actual lap of the weekend came in FP2 (1:22.679), and he could not improve on it on Saturday morning.

Behind Russell, the aggregated order is remarkably tight. Hamilton (1:22.378), Antonelli (1:22.429), Lando Norris (1:22.471) and Leclerc (1:22.474) are separated by under a tenth, with Max Verstappen (1:22.569) and Oscar Piastri (1:22.576) just behind. That is four drivers from three teams inside 0.096s — the kind of spread where a single tow or a tidy Parabolica decides the front two rows.

This is where our exclusive data matters. Official timesheets only show each driver's best single lap. By combining every driver's best sectors across all sessions, we reveal what each car is genuinely capable of — and who has been leaving time on the table. At Monza, that hidden gap separates the drivers who are already maxing out from those with something in reserve for Q3.

sections.heading: Sector-by-Sector Breakdown
sections.content:
Sector 1 — the run from the start line through the Rettifilo chicane and Curva Grande — rewards low drag and confident braking into Turn 1. Oscar Piastri was the only driver to dip under 27 seconds, a 26.981 in FP3, and it is no coincidence that the next three names are a mix of front-runners and low-drag specialists: Pierre Gasly (27.039), Russell (27.044) and Hamilton (27.046). Carlos Sainz's 27.070 for Williams is a reminder of how much a slippery car can claw back on this opening stretch.

Sector 2, covering the Roggia chicane and the two Lesmos, is where mechanical grip and traction out of slow corners show up. Norris owns it with 27.704, with Russell just 0.005s behind at 27.709. Antonelli (27.784) and Piastri (27.860) complete a sector dominated by Mercedes and McLaren. Ferrari trail here — Leclerc's 27.874 and Hamilton's 27.896 — while Verstappen's 28.027 is a clear weakness, giving up 0.323s to Norris in this sector alone.

Sector 3 — Ascari, the back straight and Parabolica — flips that story. Verstappen is fastest of all with 27.282, ahead of Arvid Lindblad's eye-catching 27.300 for Racing Bulls and Russell's 27.339. That suggests the Red Bull-powered cars are running very efficient top-speed trims, and it explains how Verstappen could sit sixth in the aggregated order despite his Sector 2 deficit. Leclerc's 27.385 is Ferrari's best showing here.

The real reason Russell leads is not a single sector but the absence of a weak one. He is top three in all three sectors: 27.044, 27.709 and 27.339. Nobody else can say that. Norris has the best Sector 2 but loses 0.321s to Verstappen in Sector 3; Piastri has the best Sector 1 but drops 0.458s to Verstappen through the final sector. Mercedes simply has the most complete package at Monza.

sections.heading: Understanding Aggregated vs Actual Times
sections.content:
The aggregated lap takes each driver's best Sector 1, best Sector 2 and best Sector 3 from across all three practice sessions — even if those sectors were set on different laps or different days — and adds them together. Russell's 1:22.092, for example, combines a Sector 1 from FP2 with Sectors 2 and 3 from FP3. The actual lap is what official timing shows: the fastest single, complete lap of the weekend.

The difference between the two is the delta. A small delta means a driver is already stringing their best sectors together; there is little hidden pace left. A large delta means the speed is clearly in the car but has not yet arrived in one lap — usually because of traffic, a mistake, a missed tow, or tyres that peaked at the wrong moment. In qualifying, with fresh softs and a clean run, drivers tend to close that gap, which is why the aggregated order is a sharper qualifying predictor than any single practice timesheet.

No official source publishes this view. It is unique to this platform, and at a track like Monza — where slipstream luck can distort single-lap times — it filters out much of the noise.

sections.heading: Practice Session Evolution
sections.content:
FP1 belonged to Ferrari. Leclerc's 1:23.008 and Hamilton's 1:23.181 led Russell (1:23.312) and Liam Lawson (1:23.433), with Verstappen sitting the session out as Ayumu Iwasa took his car. Several teams ran rookies — Paul Aron for Alpine, Luke Browning for Williams and Colton Herta for Cadillac — which thinned out the representative data early on.

FP2 was the turning point. Russell's 1:22.559 jumped to the top, 0.120s clear of Leclerc, with Antonelli third at +0.141. Verstappen's first outing produced only ninth (1:23.377), but his FP3 transformation was striking: 1:22.569, an improvement of 0.808s and good enough for third on the FP3 timesheet. Russell found another 0.340s overnight to reach 1:22.219, his total gain from FP1 to FP3 standing at 1.093s.

Ferrari's trajectory is the warning sign. Leclerc's laps went 1:23.008, 1:22.679, then 1:22.708 — no improvement in FP3. Hamilton kept progressing (1:23.181, 1:23.016, 1:22.445) and finished FP3 second. Lindblad is the other big mover: 1:23.802 in FP1, 1:23.349 in FP2 and 1:22.724 in FP3, putting Racing Bulls seventh and ahead of Piastri's best actual lap. The single-lap data does not capture long-run pace, but the volume of medium and hard running in FP1 and FP2 suggests most teams completed their race preparation on Friday.

sections.heading: Tyre Strategy Analysis
sections.content:
The front-runners kept their practice running lean: between four and eight sets each across the three sessions. Hamilton and Norris used just three sets of softs in practice, keeping the most fresh red-walled rubber in reserve. Leclerc, Russell and Piastri each went through five softs — Leclerc ran three in FP2 alone, a sign Ferrari were chasing a one-lap answer to Mercedes' Friday pace.

Every top-team driver except Verstappen logged a hard compound run, giving their engineers some data on the likely race tyre. Verstappen, who missed FP1, used only two softs and two mediums in practice and never ran the hard. That leaves Red Bull with less race-tyre information than their rivals — a potential handicap if the race turns on hard-tyre degradation.

Further back, the approaches diverged sharply. Esteban Ocon got through 15 sets in practice, including seven mediums, and Bearman ran 13 — Haas clearly prioritised race preparation. Both Audi drivers put four sets of mediums on in FP3, a late shift towards long runs. At the other end, Lance Stroll burned eight softs in practice, five of them in FP3, as Aston Martin searched for one-lap grip that never came.

Monza's long straights and low-downforce setups typically limit tyre wear, which makes a one-stop the natural race plan. Expect most of the front-runners to start on mediums and switch to hards, with the undercut less potent than usual because of the long pit-lane loss.

sections.heading: Key Findings and Surprises
sections.content:
1. Mercedes are the class of the field. Russell leads the aggregated order by 0.286s, topped two of three sessions and is the only driver in the top three of every sector. Antonelli's third place in the aggregated order (1:22.429) confirms this is a car advantage, not just a driver advantage.

2. Verstappen is the most efficient driver in the field. His aggregated and actual laps are identical at 1:22.569 — every one of his best sectors came on the same FP3 lap. He also owns the fastest Sector 3 (27.282). The flip side is that there is no hidden time left; his Sector 2 deficit is structural.

3. Racing Bulls lead the midfield. Lindblad's aggregated 1:22.640 puts him eighth overall, 0.061s ahead of Gasly (1:22.701) and almost half a second clear of the next midfield car. Behind, Colapinto (1:23.091), Lawson (1:23.125) and Hulkenberg (1:23.126) are covered by 0.035s — a three-way scramble for Q3 places.

4. Leclerc and Piastri carry the biggest hidden potential among the front-runners. Leclerc's delta is 0.205s and Piastri's is 0.197s. If both clean up their laps, they could leapfrog Antonelli and Norris in qualifying. Among the wider field, Valtteri Bottas has the largest delta of any race driver at 0.430s, while Aston Martin are the weekend's biggest concern, with Alonso (1:24.794) and Stroll (1:25.253) the slowest of the regular drivers.

sections.heading: Race Day Predictions
sections.content:
Qualifying Prediction: Based on the aggregated order, we expect pole in the 1:21.9–1:22.0 range, with Russell's theoretical 1:22.092 already within reach before fresh softs and a lower fuel load. Our predicted top three: Russell, Hamilton, Antonelli. Watch Leclerc (0.205s delta) and Piastri (0.197s) — they have the most unused pace among front-runners and are the likeliest to crash the front row.

Race Prediction: Russell to win. He combines the best aggregated lap with the most complete sector profile, and the Mercedes looks strong in the traction zones that matter for defending out of the chicanes. Expect a one-stop, medium to hard, with the pit window opening around the middle of the race. Ferrari's home crowd will push Hamilton hard, but the Mercedes advantage through Sector 2 is hard to overcome over a full stint.

Podium Prediction: 1. George Russell (Mercedes), 2. Lewis Hamilton (Ferrari), 3. Lando Norris (McLaren). Norris's best-in-field Sector 2 should make him tough to pass, and McLaren's balanced practice tyre programme gives them solid race data.

Wildcard Factors: Monza's slipstream can scramble qualifying, and contact at the Rettifilo on lap one is a recurring risk, bringing a real chance of an early safety car. Verstappen's lack of hard-tyre running is another unknown. Dark Horse: Arvid Lindblad. His Sector 3 of 27.300 is second only to Verstappen, and if the Racing Bulls top speed translates into the race, a top-six finish is realistic.

Key Battle to Watch: Hamilton vs Leclerc. The Ferrari team-mates are split by just 0.096s in our aggregated order, and Leclerc carries three times Hamilton's delta. At Ferrari's home race, the fight for intra-team supremacy could be as gripping as the battle for the win.
